widgets.expected_heading: The Yalta Conference at the Peak of Unity

concept_widget.title: The Yalta Conference (February 1945): Three Grand Alliance Agreements & One Sharp Faultline
concept_widget.caption: Click each summit dossier to compare what Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin agreed at Yalta in February 1945—and why Poland already exposed deep division.

items.title: Four-Power Occupation of Germany & Berlin
items.takeaway: With Nazi defeat imminent, the Big Three agreed to divide both defeated Germany and Berlin—deep inside the Soviet zone—into four occupation zones.

items.title: German Reparations & War Against Japan

metrics.label: Pacific Pledge
metrics.value: USSR Joins War 3 Months After V-E

items.takeaway: The Allies set German reparations at $20 billion (half going to the USSR), while Stalin confirmed Soviet entry against Japan within three months of German surrender.

items.title: Declaration on Liberated Europe
items.takeaway: Even though Red Army troops already occupied much of Eastern Europe, Stalin signed the Declaration on Liberated Europe promising free elections across liberated nations.

items.title: The Polish Faultline: Lublin Poles vs London Poles
items.takeaway: With Red Army troops already in Poland, Stalin insisted on recognising the pro-Soviet Lublin Poles to secure a buffer zone, clashing with Churchill’s support for the exiled London Poles.

concept_widget.title: Stalin’s Eastern Bloc Consolidation (1947–1949): Cominform ↔ Expulsion of Tito ↔ Comecon
concept_widget.caption: Slide or click across the three pillars to see how Stalin countered the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan by locking Eastern Europe into an ideological and economic bloc.

stops.label: 1. Cominform: Moscow’s Ideological Command Bureau (September 1947)
stops.summary: Established in September 1947 to counter the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, Cominform placed European Communist parties under Moscow’s strict ideological direction and ordered strikes against Marshall Aid.

stops.label: 2. Disciplining Defiance: Yugoslavia Expelled from Cominform (1948)
stops.summary: When Marshal Josip Broz Tito insisted on running Communist Yugoslavia independently rather than taking Stalin’s orders, Cominform expelled Yugoslavia in 1948 as a warning to all satellite leaders.

stops.label: 3. Comecon: Economic Integration & Trade Wall (January 1949)
stops.summary: Created in January 1949 as Moscow’s answer to Marshall Aid, Comecon specialised Eastern Bloc production around Soviet priorities while cutting off trade with Western Europe.

traits.value: Cut Off Trade with Western Europe

widgets.expected_heading: The Nuclear Arms Race & The Warsaw Pact (1949–55)

concept_widget.title: Nuclear & Alliance Escalation (1949–1957): From Soviet A-Bomb to Warsaw Pact & ICBMs
concept_widget.caption: Click each milestone from August 1949 to 1957 to watch the US nuclear monopoly give way to thermonuclear H-bombs, rival European military alliances, and long-range missiles.

eras.headline: Soviet Atomic Bomb Ends US Four-Year Monopoly
eras.summary: In August 1949, the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb, ending America’s four-year nuclear monopoly and dramatically intensifying superpower rivalry.

eras.headline: Superpowers Detonate Rival Hydrogen Bombs (1,000x Hiroshima)
eras.summary: Determined to stay ahead, the USA detonated an H-bomb in November 1952 (roughly 1,000 times Hiroshima), matched within nine months by a Soviet H-bomb in August 1953.

eras.headline: West Germany Joins NATO & Khrushchev Forms Warsaw Pact
eras.summary: When NATO admitted a rearmed West Germany (FRG) in May 1955, Nikita Khrushchev founded the Warsaw Pact on 14 May 1955, uniting the USSR and seven Eastern European satellites under Soviet command.

eras.headline: Soviet ICBMs Place North America Within Strike Range
eras.summary: By 1957, Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) could strike North America directly, locking Europe and both superpowers into two nuclear-armed camps.

pillars.status: North America Now Reachable by Missile

widgets.expected_heading: The East German Refugee Crisis & Brain Drain

concept_widget.title: Why Millions Fled East (1949–1961): West Berlin Showcase ↔ GDR ‘Brain Drain’ ↔ Nov 1958 Ultimatum
concept_widget.caption: Slide or click across the three stages to see why 2.7 to 3 million East Germans fled through West Berlin—and why Khrushchev issued his six-month Berlin Ultimatum on 27 November 1958.

stops.label: 1. Prosperous Capitalist ‘Window to the West’ (1950s)
stops.summary: Boosted by Marshall Plan investment deep inside Communist East Germany, West Berlin showcased abundant consumer goods, higher living standards, and democratic freedoms.

traits.value: Open Crossing to Fly to FRG

stops.label: 2. Stasi Repression & The 2.7–3 Million ‘Brain Drain’ (1949–1961)
stops.summary: Fleeing low wages, forced collectivisation, and Stasi repression under unpopular GDR leader Walter Ulbricht, 2.7 to 3 million citizens—including young doctors, engineers, and teachers—left East Germany.

stops.label: 3. Khrushchev’s Six-Month Berlin Ultimatum (27 November 1958)
stops.summary: With the GDR nearing economic collapse, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev issued his Berlin Ultimatum on 27 November 1958, demanding Western troops withdraw within six months to leave a demilitarised ‘free city’.

traits.value: Six Months for West to Withdraw

concept_widget.title: 14–24 October 1962: Kennedy’s ExComm Options After U-2 Photos of San Cristóbal
concept_widget.caption: After U-2 photos on 14 October revealed R-12 (SS-4) missile sites in Cuba with a ten-minute strike window on Washington, slide across the three responses weighed by ExComm.

stops.label: 1. Diplomatic Protest Only (Rejected as Too Weak)
stops.summary: Relying on diplomatic protest alone avoided immediate military clash, but ExComm warned it would leave Soviet R-12 medium-range nuclear missiles operational within ten minutes of major US cities.

traits.value: U-2 Photos of San Cristóbal Sites

stops.label: 2. 500-Mile Naval ‘Quarantine’ & DEFCON 2 (22–24 October 1962)
stops.summary: On 22 October, Kennedy exposed the bases on TV, raised US forces to DEFCON 2, and ordered a 500-mile naval ‘quarantine’ (avoiding the warlike term blockade)—prompting Soviet missile ships to turn back on 24 October.

stops.label: 3. Immediate Airstrikes & Invasion of Cuba (Rejected Hawk Option)
stops.summary: Bombing San Cristóbal and invading Cuba promised to destroy the launch pads directly, but risked killing Soviet troops on the ground and igniting full-scale nuclear war.

traits.value: Held Back in Favour of Quarantine

widgets.expected_heading: The Warsaw Pact Invasion of August 1968

concept_widget.title: 20–21 August 1968: How 500,000 Warsaw Pact Troops Seized Czechoslovakia
concept_widget.caption: Click each stage to trace the Soviet Politburo’s 17 August decision, the overnight four-nation invasion, and Moscow’s fabricated ‘fraternal assistance’ claim.

items.title: Failed Summits & The Politburo Invasion Vote
items.takeaway: Convinced after the Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava summits that Alexander Dubček would never reimpose censorship or silence anti-Soviet newspapers, the Soviet Politburo voted on 17 August for armed intervention.

items.title: 500,000 Troops & Seizure of Ruzyňe Airport
items.takeaway: Late on 20–21 August 1968, tanks painted with white invasion stripes rumbled into Prague while Soviet paratroopers seized Ruzyňe Airport after a transport plane requested an emergency landing.

items.title: Moscow’s Unsigned Appeal & Svoboda’s Barracks Order
items.takeaway: Although Moscow’s state news agency claimed Czechoslovak Communists had requested ‘fraternal assistance’, no senior leader had signed it, and President Ludvík Svoboda kept the army in barracks to prevent bloodshed.

concept_widget.title: Why Both Superpowers Wanted Détente (1970–1972): US Pressures ↔ Shared MAD Fear ↔ Soviet Needs
concept_widget.caption: Slide or click across the three sets of pressures to compare why Washington and Moscow both sought a relaxation of Cold War tension in the early 1970s.

stops.label: 1. American Pressures: Vietnam Drain, Inflation & Protest (Early 1970s)
stops.summary: Under President Richard Nixon and adviser Henry Kissinger, the USA was drained by the Vietnam War—costing over $150 billion, killing 58,000 Americans, fuelling inflation, and sparking fierce protests.

stops.label: 2. Mutual Incentive: Avoiding MAD & Curbing Arms Spending (Post-1962)
stops.summary: Ever since the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, both superpowers feared Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and having reached rough nuclear parity, both wanted to curb ruinous arms spending.

stops.label: 3. Soviet Pressures: Stagnant Living Standards & The China Split (1970–72)
stops.summary: Leonid Brezhnev needed Western grain imports and industrial technology for stagnant Soviet living standards, while fearing isolation after the Sino-Soviet split and Nixon’s February 1972 visit to China.

widgets.expected_heading: Crisis in Kabul & The Soviet Invasion

concept_widget.title: April 1978 – December 1979: Why Brezhnev Invaded Afghanistan
concept_widget.caption: Click each stage from the April 1978 Saur Revolution to the December 1979 Kabul assault to see why Brezhnev intervened—and trapped the USSR in a ten-year war.

items.title: PDPA Takeover & Mujahideen Rebellion
items.takeaway: After the April 1978 Saur Revolution brought Nur Muhammad Taraki’s pro-Soviet PDPA to power, radical land and secular reforms provoked fierce armed rebellion from Islamic Mujahideen guerrillas.

items.title: Hafizullah Amin Murders Taraki & Seizes Power
items.takeaway: In September 1979, Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin seized power and had Taraki murdered, while Moscow suspected the unpredictable Amin of secretly contacting the USA.

items.title: Iranian Spillover Fear & The Brezhnev Doctrine
items.takeaway: Watching the 1979 Iranian Revolution next door, Leonid Brezhnev feared Islamic fundamentalism spreading into 30 million Soviet Central Asian Muslims and invoked the Brezhnev Doctrine.

items.title: Soviet Forces Storm Kabul & Install Babrak Karmal
items.takeaway: Between 24 and 27 December 1979, Soviet airborne and armoured forces stormed Kabul’s presidential palace, killed Amin, and installed Moscow-backed Babrak Karmal—starting a costly ten-year war.

widgets.expected_heading: Eastern European Revolutions, Reunification & The Warsaw Pact

concept_widget.title: Unravelling the Soviet Bloc (Nov 1989 – 1 July 1991): Revolutions, Reunification & End of the Warsaw Pact
concept_widget.caption: Click each turning point after the opening of the Berlin Wall to watch Communist rule collapse across Eastern Europe, Germany reunite inside NATO, and the Warsaw Pact dissolve.

eras.headline: Domino Collapse Across Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria & Romania
eras.summary: Czechoslovakia’s peaceful Velvet Revolution made playwright Václav Havel president, Bulgaria ousted Todor Zhivkov, and Romania’s violent December uprising overthrew and executed Nicolae Ceaușescu.

eras.headline: Formal German Reunification Inside NATO
eras.summary: Backed by Western financial loans, Chancellor Helmut Kohl won Mikhail Gorbachev’s consent for formal German reunification on 3 October 1990, with a united democratic Germany remaining inside NATO.

eras.headline: Warsaw Pact Military Structures & Alliance Dissolved
eras.summary: After elected governments in Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia demanded Soviet troop withdrawal, Warsaw Pact military structures dissolved in March 1991 and the alliance formally ended on 1 July 1991.
